prompt.brief: Design a cost-optimized batch-processing platform that accepts large workloads, schedules them across elastic workers, produces durable results, and keeps compute spend low without sacrificing correctness or predictable completion times.
successSignals: Separate durable job intent and input data from ephemeral compute.
Use queues, capacity-aware scheduling, checkpointing, retries, and idempotent outputs.
Optimize cost with spot or preemptible capacity, autoscaling, rightsizing, and storage lifecycle policies.
Define completion SLAs, fairness, tenant quotas, observability, and cheap-capacity fallback behavior.

functional: Submit, validate, pause, cancel, retry, and inspect tenant-owned batch jobs.
Support dependencies, priorities, resource requirements, deadlines, retries, checkpoints, and partial progress.
Stage inputs, execute tasks on elastic workers, persist outputs, and expose logs, metrics, and completion status.
Allow budgets, quotas, regions, data-retention policies, and maximum completion windows.
nonFunctional: A submitted job and terminal state must be durable; duplicate execution must not duplicate committed outputs.
Meet a configurable completion SLA, such as 95% of standard jobs completing within 30 minutes.
Minimize cost while maintaining isolation, fairness, data security, and urgent-work capacity.
Tolerate worker preemption, zone failure, queue backlog, malformed tasks, slow tenants, and object-store throttling.
scaleAssumptions: 10,000 tenants submit 1 million jobs per day, with 20,000 runnable tasks at peak.
Inputs and outputs total 5 PB per month; most data is immutable and lifecycle-tiered.
Use on-demand capacity for deadlines and spot or preemptible capacity for retryable workloads.
Jobs range from seconds to hours; avoid one queue or database partition becoming the bottleneck.

metrics.label: Peak runnable tasks
metrics.description: Drives queue partitioning, scheduler throughput, and worker-pool autoscaling.

metrics.label: Completion SLA
metrics.description: Cheap capacity is used until deadline risk requires on-demand capacity.

metrics.label: Cost target
metrics.description: Prefer preemptible capacity for checkpointable work and fall back when SLA risk rises.

metrics.label: Data growth
metrics.description: Requires lifecycle tiers, locality-aware scheduling, and bounded intermediate data.

entities.name: BatchJob
entities.notes: Durable job intent and policy; state transitions are conditional and idempotent.

entities.name: TaskAttempt
entities.notes: An attempt is disposable and retryable; leases prevent two workers committing the same attempt.

entities.name: Artifact
entities.notes: Content-addressed outputs make retries safe and enable deduplication and lifecycle movement.

entities.name: CapacityPolicy
entities.notes: Versioned policy controls cost, capacity selection, tenant quotas, and fallback thresholds.

apis.contract: { inputUri, tasks, dependencies, priority, deadline, budget, requestId } -> { jobId, state }
apis.notes: Authenticate the tenant, validate the DAG and resource limits, and persist the job idempotently.

apis.contract: { state, progress, cost, attempts, outputs, updatedAt }
apis.notes: Return durable state plus eventually consistent telemetry and explicit progress timestamps.
Record cancellation durably; workers stop at a safe checkpoint.
Grant a bounded lease; the worker heartbeats and commits output conditionally.

dataFlow.title: Accept the batch job
dataFlow.description: The API validates the tenant, input manifest, DAG, resource limits, budget, and deadline, then writes durable job intent.

dataFlow.title: Stage and partition work
dataFlow.description: A planner resolves dependencies, creates task records, groups compatible work, and places input metadata near eligible pools.

dataFlow.title: Schedule cost-aware capacity
dataFlow.description: The scheduler chooses spot capacity when checkpointing and deadline slack allow it, reserving on-demand capacity as SLA risk rises.

dataFlow.title: Lease, checkpoint, and commit
dataFlow.description: Workers claim fenced leases, heartbeat progress, write checkpoints and content-addressed outputs, and conditionally commit one successful attempt.

dataFlow.title: Reconcile and report asynchronously
dataFlow.description: A reconciler expires leases, retries safe tasks, releases idle capacity, updates cost and progress telemetry, and archives artifacts by policy.

architecture.title: Cost-optimized batch-processing reference architecture
architecture.summary: Durable job intent and object-backed artifacts feed a deadline-aware scheduler. Elastic worker pools use cheap preemptible capacity where safe, with checkpointed retries and on-demand fallback for SLA protection.

layers.label: Control plane
layers.description: Submission, job lifecycle, policy, and tenant quotas.

layers.label: Scheduling plane
layers.description: Planning, dependency tracking, queues, and capacity selection.

layers.label: Execution and data plane
layers.description: Checkpointable workers and durable content-addressed artifacts.

layers.label: Operations
layers.description: Retries, cost telemetry, retention, and SLA monitoring.

keyPaths.label: Submission path
keyPaths.description: Client -> gateway -> job service -> durable job store.

keyPaths.label: Execution path
keyPaths.description: Planner -> queue -> cost-aware scheduler -> workers -> artifacts.

keyPaths.label: Recovery path
keyPaths.description: Leases and telemetry -> reconciler -> retry or capacity policy changes.

components.label: Tenant clients
components.description: Submit jobs and inspect state, progress, cost, logs, and artifacts.

components.label: API gateway
components.description: Authenticates tenants, enforces quotas, validates payloads, and rate-limits control operations.

components.label: Job service
components.description: Owns job lifecycle, DAG validation, cancellation, authorization, and idempotent transitions.

components.label: Job metadata store
components.description: Durable source of truth for jobs, tasks, attempts, policies, and terminal results.

components.label: DAG planner
components.description: Expands dependencies and creates only dependency-ready task batches.

components.label: Partitioned task queues
components.description: Prioritized queues partitioned by tenant, resource class, locality, and deadline risk.

components.label: Cost-aware scheduler
components.description: Matches tasks to capacity using price, preemption risk, locality, fairness, and deadline slack.

components.label: Elastic capacity manager
components.description: Requests, drains, and rightsizes preemptible and on-demand worker pools.

components.label: Checkpointable workers
components.description: Execute leased tasks, heartbeat progress, checkpoint state, and commit outputs idempotently.

components.label: Artifact object store
components.description: Stores immutable inputs, outputs, logs, and manifests with checksums and lifecycle tiers.

components.label: Checkpoint and lease store
components.description: Stores task progress, lease ownership, checkpoint pointers, and attempt fencing state.

components.label: Reconciler
components.description: Expires leases, retries safe failures, detects stuck DAGs, and repairs incomplete state.

components.label: Cost and usage meter
components.description: Attributes compute, storage, and egress cost by tenant, job, pool, and policy.

components.label: SLA and operations
components.description: Tracks queue age, deadline risk, utilization, preemption, cost, and correctness.

connections.label: Job command
connections.description: Tenant submits or inspects a batch job.

connections.label: Durable job state
connections.description: Persists job intent, tasks, attempts, policy, and terminal state.

connections.label: Task batch
connections.description: Queues work by priority, resource class, locality, and deadline.

connections.label: Scheduling demand
connections.description: Scheduler considers backlog, capacity, and cost policy.

connections.label: Capacity request
connections.description: Requests cheap or on-demand capacity based on SLA risk.

connections.label: Task lease
connections.description: Assigns a fenced, time-bounded task attempt.

connections.label: Outputs and logs
connections.description: Writes checksummed immutable artifacts and logs.

connections.label: Lease and checkpoint
connections.description: Heartbeats and checkpoints make preemption recovery safe.

connections.label: Expired attempts
connections.description: Reconciler retries or marks failures according to policy.

connections.label: Retry task
connections.description: Requeues safe work with bounded backoff.

connections.label: Usage events
connections.description: Attributes compute and preemption cost asynchronously.

connections.label: Backlog and age
connections.description: Monitors queue pressure and deadline risk.

deepDives.title: Cost optimization without SLA surprises
points: Use spot or preemptible capacity for checkpointable work and on-demand capacity for deadlines, non-retryable tasks, and recovery bursts.
Scale on queue age, deadline slack, and expected task duration rather than CPU utilization alone.
Measure cost per successful output including retries, idle drain time, storage, egress, and operational overhead.

deepDives.title: Checkpointing and exactly-once effects
points: Workers may execute at least once, but content-addressed outputs and conditional commit make visible results idempotent.
Fence expired workers with lease versions so a delayed attempt cannot commit after another succeeds.
Choose checkpoint granularity from recomputation cost and checkpoint storage overhead.

deepDives.title: Fairness and tenant isolation
points: Use weighted fair queues, per-tenant concurrency limits, budgets, and noisy-neighbor protection.
Partition scheduler state so a large tenant cannot monopolize a global lock or starve urgent small jobs.
Expose cost attribution and policy decisions so budget failures are explainable.

deepDives.title: Data lifecycle and recovery
points: Keep immutable artifacts in object storage with checksums, lifecycle tiers, retention policies, and region restrictions.
Rebuild projections from durable job state and manifests, not worker-local disks or queue messages.
Test zone failure, object-store throttling, scheduler restart, mass preemption, and partial DAG completion.

tradeoffs.title: Spot-first versus on-demand capacity
tradeoffs.recommendation: Use spot-first for checkpointable work and switch based on deadline risk, preemption rate, and recovery cost.
tradeoffs.caution: Always using the cheapest instance can miss SLAs through repeated preemption or queue starvation.

tradeoffs.title: Central scheduler versus decentralized claims
tradeoffs.recommendation: Use partitioned scheduling decisions with queue leases for predictable fairness and a bounded control plane.
tradeoffs.caution: A global scheduler becomes a bottleneck; fully decentralized claims make fairness and cost policy difficult.

tradeoffs.title: Recompute versus checkpoint
tradeoffs.recommendation: Checkpoint when recomputation cost exceeds checkpoint storage and write cost; otherwise retry from immutable inputs.
tradeoffs.caution: Checkpointing every small step can cost more than the work and create object-store pressure.

commonMistakes: Treating worker-local state as durable and losing progress after preemption.
Optimizing instance price while ignoring retries, idle capacity, storage, egress, and missed-SLA cost.
Using one global queue or lock for every tenant and resource class.
Claiming exactly-once execution instead of making commits and artifacts idempotent.
Leaving budgets, fairness, cancellation, retention, and deadline fallback unspecified.

followUps.question: What happens when a job is close to its deadline but only spot capacity is available?
followUps.answer: Estimate remaining work and preemption risk, then escalate critical tasks to on-demand capacity while preserving checkpointed progress.

followUps.question: How would you support streaming or interactive jobs?
followUps.answer: Use a separate latency-sensitive pool and admission policy rather than weakening batch fairness and cost controls.

followUps.question: How do you prevent duplicate outputs after a retry?
followUps.answer: Use deterministic task and output keys, checksums, conditional commit with attempt fencing, and one canonical successful attempt.

followUps.question: How do you prove the platform is cost optimized?
followUps.answer: Compare cost per successful output and SLA attainment across policies, including retry and storage costs, using replayable simulations.

rubric.description: Includes preemptible capacity, autoscaling, retry cost, storage lifecycle, egress, and cost per successful output.
Durable intent, leases, checkpoints, idempotent outputs, fencing, retries, and terminal state are explicit.
Dependencies, priorities, fairness, quotas, deadlines, queue partitioning, and hot-tenant isolation are covered.
Preemption, worker and zone failure, object-store issues, reconciliation, replay, and degraded capacity are addressed.
SLA, backlog, utilization, spend attribution, policy explainability, logs, metrics, and retention are observable.
